The household survives through duty and sacrifice, but its members become increasingly isolated from one another.

Philip meets Maggie secretly in the Red Deeps and argues that her harsh self-denial is another form of narrowness. Their shared love of books, music, and conversation revives her, and Philip declares his love. Maggie cannot promise marriage, but she acknowledges their bond. Tom discovers the meetings and orders Maggie to end them, insisting that loyalty to their father makes any connection with a Wakem impossible. She yields, though she rejects Tom's claim to govern her conscience. Tom's commercial efforts eventually allow the family debts to be paid in full, restoring Mr. Tulliver's pride. The success does not end his obsession with Wakem. In a chance encounter he attacks and horsewhips the lawyer, then collapses and dies soon afterward. Tom assumes responsibility for the family and remains determined to recover the mill, while Maggie leaves home to work as a governess, carrying grief, frustrated affection, and a deepening estrangement from her brother.

Years later Maggie visits Lucy Deane in St. Ogg's. Lucy hopes to bring her together again with Philip and is herself informally attached to Stephen Guest, a confident young businessman. Stephen and Maggie feel an immediate attraction, despite their obligations to Lucy and Philip. Their meetings become emotionally dangerous even as both try to preserve outward loyalty. Philip persuades his father to consider selling Dorlcote Mill to the Guest firm so that Tom may recover it, and Tom succeeds in buying back the family home. This achievement does not soften his authority over Maggie. When he learns that Philip still loves her, he repeats his opposition, though he cannot deny that Philip helped make the purchase possible. Maggie tries to leave St. Ogg's before her feeling for Stephen causes harm, but Lucy arranges further contact, unaware that the attraction she is encouraging is not between Maggie and Philip alone.

Maggie and Stephen struggle against their attraction, each recognizing that acting on it would betray Lucy and Philip. During a planned boat outing, Stephen takes Philip's place and allows the current to carry him and Maggie far beyond their intended return point. By the time Maggie understands how deliberately he has prolonged the journey, returning at once is impractical and their unexplained absence already threatens scandal. Stephen urges her to continue with him and marry, arguing that their love justifies breaking the expectations around them. Maggie briefly yields to the prospect, then concludes that happiness founded on injury to Lucy and Philip would violate her deepest obligations. She leaves Stephen before marriage and returns alone to face St. Ogg's. Her choice protects the commitments she values, but its outward circumstances make it look as though she first eloped and then abandoned him.

St. Ogg's condemns Maggie after her return, judging the appearance of her journey rather than her refusal to marry Stephen. Tom denies her a place in the recovered family home. Bob Jakin and his wife shelter her, while the clergyman Dr. Kenn supports her and helps her find work. Philip writes with compassion, and Lucy comes privately to forgive her, easing Maggie's fear that her choice destroyed them. Stephen also writes, still urging a shared future, but Maggie maintains her refusal. Exceptional rain then sends a destructive flood down the Floss. Maggie rows through the current to Dorlcote Mill and rescues Tom. In the crisis he understands her love, and brother and sister are reconciled. They try to reach Lucy and the Deanes, but wreckage from the flooded riverside strikes their boat. Maggie and Tom drown holding each other. They are buried together; years afterward Philip visits their grave alone, while Lucy and Stephen remember them together.

characters.description: A young Alabama girl left deaf and blind by an illness in infancy. Nearly seven when the main action begins, she is intelligent, strong-willed, and eager to understand her surroundings, but has no shared language beyond a few signs she has devised at home. Her frustrated outbursts dominate the Keller household until Annie Sullivan arrives to teach her.
characters.name: Helen Keller

characters.description: A young teacher sent from the Perkins Institution to work with Helen. Partially sighted after operations and marked by a harsh childhood in an almshouse, she brings energy, persistence, and unconventional methods to her first teaching post. She believes Helen needs disciplined instruction and language rather than pity.
characters.name: Anne Sullivan

characters.description: Helen's devoted mother, who continues to search for help when others have nearly accepted that nothing can be done. She understands many of Helen's improvised signs and is torn between protecting her child from distress and giving Annie the authority to teach her.
characters.name: Kate Keller

characters.description: Helen's father, a former Confederate officer and newspaper editor who expects order in his household. He loves Helen but doubts that a young Northern teacher can reach her, and Annie's blunt manner quickly puts them at odds.
characters.name: Arthur Keller

characters.description: Captain Keller's adult son from his first marriage and Helen's older half-brother. He masks resentment and uncertainty with sarcasm, frequently challenging his father while watching Annie's struggle with skeptical interest.
characters.name: James Keller

characters.description: Helen's talkative aunt, affectionate toward the family and convinced that some form of expert help must exist. Her suggestion that the Kellers contact a specialist helps bring Annie to Alabama.
characters.name: Evelyn

characters.description: The director of the Perkins Institution and Annie's mentor. At Annie's farewell he acknowledges both her difficult past and her promise as a teacher, while warning that knowledge alone will not make her patient.
characters.name: Michael Anagnos

characters.description: A household servant in the Keller home and mother of Martha and Percy. She assists the family in caring for Helen and observes the upheaval caused by Annie's arrival.
characters.name: Viney

characters.description: Viney's young daughter and one of Helen's regular playmates. She has learned to accommodate Helen's forceful way of communicating, though their games can turn rough when Helen becomes frustrated.
characters.name: Martha

characters.description: Viney's son, a younger child in the Keller household. Annie later uses his presence and Helen's curiosity about him as part of her early teaching efforts.
characters.name: Percy

recaps.ending: At the pump, Helen suddenly understands that Annie's hand movements name the water flowing over her other hand. She races around the grounds asking for the names of everything she touches, reconnects with her parents through this new language, and tries to say the word for water aloud. She also returns the key she had hidden after locking Annie in her room. Finally Helen asks Annie's name; Annie spells teacher into her hand. The breakthrough resolves the central struggle over whether Helen can connect symbols with the world. The family sees that Annie's discipline has opened a path to communication, while Annie recognizes that affection and trust can now join the lessons she has fought to establish.
recaps.in_short: After an illness leaves infant Helen Keller unable to see or hear, her loving family struggles to control or communicate with her. When Helen is nearly seven, the Perkins Institution sends Anne Sullivan, a young teacher with impaired sight and a painful past. Annie immediately begins spelling words into Helen's hand, but Helen imitates the motions without understanding that they carry meaning. Annie also challenges the family's habit of yielding to every outburst and wins permission to teach Helen in isolation. After weeks of discipline and finger-spelling, Helen still has not grasped the purpose of words. A confrontation at the family table leads Annie to take her to the outdoor pump. As water runs over Helen's hand, she recalls an early word and realizes that Annie's signs name things. Helen eagerly seeks more names and identifies Annie as teacher, beginning the shared language that will transform her life.

recaps.text: An illness in infancy leaves Helen Keller deaf and blind. Several years later she is an energetic, frustrated child who communicates through a handful of home signs and is accustomed to getting her way through physical outbursts. Her mother, Kate, remains convinced that Helen can be educated, while her father, Captain Keller, is doubtful. The family contacts the Perkins Institution, whose director, Michael Anagnos, sends Anne Sullivan to Alabama for her first teaching position. Annie has limited sight and memories of a severe childhood, but she is determined not to let pity govern Helen's life. She begins spelling words into Helen's palm and gives her a doll, though Helen copies the finger motions without understanding them. Helen tests the newcomer, strikes her, and eventually locks her in an upstairs room. Captain Keller has to rescue Annie by ladder, while Helen secretly disposes of the key. The episode establishes both Helen's ingenuity and the resistance Annie must overcome.

Annie concludes that Helen cannot learn while the family rewards her disruptions. During a long breakfast struggle she makes Helen sit at the table, eat with a spoon, and fold her napkin, refusing to surrender even when the lesson becomes exhausting and physical. The victory convinces Annie that consistent boundaries are possible, but Kate and Captain Keller are distressed by her severity. Annie asks to live alone with Helen in the garden house for a limited period, with the family kept out of sight, so Helen must depend on her teacher. The Kellers reluctantly agree. In isolation Annie builds a daily routine and steadily expands Helen's store of finger-spelled signs. Helen learns the motions quickly and becomes more manageable, but she still treats the signs as a game of imitation rather than as names with meaning. Annie worries that time is running out before the family reclaims Helen and resumes its old habits.

Helen returns to the main house with improved manners, but at a celebratory meal she tests whether the old rules still apply. When she spills a pitcher, Annie insists that she refill it and takes her outside to the pump. As water pours across one of Helen's hands, Annie spells its name into the other. The sensation revives Helen's earliest memory of language, and she finally understands that the hand signs stand for things. She moves urgently from object to object asking Annie to name each one, then identifies her mother and father. Helen retrieves the key she had hidden and gives it to Annie, a sign of their changed relationship. When she asks who Annie is, Annie spells teacher. Helen embraces her, and Annie answers with the sign for love. The family now understands that Helen can acquire language, and Annie's difficult campaign of discipline and repetition gives way to a relationship founded on communication and trust.

characters.description: A finely made china rabbit with jointed limbs, real rabbit-fur ears and tail, and an extensive wardrobe. Edward belongs to Abilene Tulane and enjoys being admired, but at the start he is vain, emotionally distant, and more concerned with his appearance than with the people who love him.
characters.name: Edward Tulane

characters.description: The girl who owns Edward and loves him wholeheartedly. Abilene dresses him carefully, includes him in family life, and speaks to him as a trusted companion even though he gives no sign of returning her devotion.
characters.name: Abilene Tulane

characters.description: Abilene's grandmother, a formidable woman who recognizes Edward's indifference to the child who loves him. She tells Abilene and Edward a severe fairy tale about a princess incapable of love, directing its warning as much toward the rabbit as toward the girl.
characters.name: Pellegrina

characters.description: An elderly fisherman who pulls Edward up from the ocean floor in his net. Lawrence brings the rabbit home rather than discarding him, beginning a new stage of Edward's life far from Abilene.
characters.name: Lawrence

characters.description: Lawrence's wife, who welcomes the recovered rabbit into their cottage, dresses him in a woman's clothes, and calls him Susanna. Her daily conversation and tenderness give Edward his first experience of being loved in a home other than Abilene's.
characters.name: Nellie

characters.description: Lawrence and Nellie's adult daughter. Lolly resents her mother's attachment to the china rabbit and treats Edward as an object rather than a member of the household.
characters.name: Lolly

characters.description: A wandering man who finds Edward after Lucy carries the rabbit from a rubbish heap. Bull gives him the name Malone, makes space for him beside the campfire, and takes him along on years of travel by rail and road.
characters.name: Bull

characters.description: Bull's loyal dog, who discovers Edward in a rubbish heap and refuses to leave him behind. Lucy's simple attachment helps bring the discarded rabbit into another makeshift family.
characters.name: Lucy

characters.description: A poor boy who finds Edward being used as a scarecrow and carries him home. Bryce works to support his gravely ill younger sister and hopes the rabbit can bring her comfort.
characters.name: Bryce

characters.description: Bryce's younger sister, weakened by a serious illness and often left alone while he works. She calls the china rabbit Jangles and loves him with a quiet intensity that Edward has finally learned to value.
characters.name: Sarah Ruth

characters.description: The owner of a Memphis diner where Bryce tries to earn money by making Edward dance for customers. Neal is impatient with the children and demands payment for the food they cannot afford.
characters.name: Neal

characters.description: A skilled doll mender who repairs Edward after the rabbit's china head is shattered. Lucius expects payment for his craft and keeps Edward in his shop when Bryce cannot meet the cost.
characters.name: Lucius Clarke

characters.description: A very old doll who shares the shop shelf with Edward. Worn by time and waiting for someone to choose her, she challenges his wish to close himself against any more love or loss.
characters.name: The Old Doll

characters.description: A young girl who enters Lucius Clarke's shop and is immediately drawn to Edward. Her arrival with her mother gives the long-waiting rabbit one more chance to be chosen and loved.
characters.name: Maggie

recaps.ending: After Sarah Ruth dies, Bryce takes Edward to Memphis and tries to support them by making the rabbit dance. A diner owner shatters Edward's china head when Bryce cannot pay for their meal. Doll mender Lucius Clarke repairs Edward but keeps him because Bryce cannot afford the work. Edward then spends years on a shelf, grieving the people he has lost and refusing to hope for another bond. An old doll tells him that a heart must remain open if anyone is ever to arrive. Eventually a girl named Maggie chooses him. Her mother is the grown Abilene, who recognizes the rabbit she lost in childhood by his familiar features and pocket watch. Edward is reunited with his first owner and accepted by her daughter. Having passed through many names, homes, separations, and forms of love, he returns to the Tulane family able at last to love the people who love him.
recaps.in_short: Edward Tulane is a beautiful china rabbit owned by Abilene, a girl who adores him, but he begins with little capacity to love her back. Lost overboard during an ocean voyage, he spends months beneath the sea before passing through many hands. Fisherman Lawrence and his wife Nellie call him Susanna; the wanderer Bull and his dog Lucy call him Malone; and poor Bryce gives him to his dying sister Sarah Ruth, who calls him Jangles. Each person loves Edward, and every separation teaches him both attachment and grief. After Sarah Ruth's death, a diner owner breaks Edward's head. Doll mender Lucius Clarke repairs him and keeps him in a shop, where Edward waits for years and nearly abandons hope. A little girl named Maggie finally chooses him. Her mother is the now-grown Abilene, who recognizes her lost rabbit. Edward returns to his original family transformed by the journey and capable of receiving and returning love.

recaps.text: Edward Tulane is an elegant china rabbit who lives with Abilene Tulane. Abilene loves him, dresses him, seats him at meals, and carries him through her days, but Edward's inner life is dominated by vanity and impatience. Abilene's grandmother Pellegrina sees that he does not return the child's love. One evening she tells a fairy tale about a beautiful princess who loves no one and is punished for her coldness. When the story ends without comforting redemption, Pellegrina makes clear that its warning is meant for Edward. He remains proud of his clothes and appearance, but for the first time he has been confronted with the emptiness of a life closed to affection.

The Tulane family sails to England with Edward. On the ship, two boys seize the rabbit from Abilene and toss him between them. During the struggle Edward is thrown overboard. Abilene is left screaming above while he sinks to the ocean floor, unable to move or call for help. He lies in darkness for hundreds of days as the sea gradually strips away his clothes and his confidence. The long isolation introduces him to fear, memory, and longing. At last a storm shifts him into the path of a fisherman's net. Lawrence pulls him from the water and brings the battered rabbit home, ending Edward's first and longest period of abandonment.

Lawrence's wife Nellie cleans Edward, dresses him in a dress, and calls him Susanna. Edward initially objects inwardly to being treated as a girl, but Nellie's conversation and steady care begin to matter more to him than the name or clothes. He listens to Lawrence and Nellie and experiences their small home as a place where he belongs. Their adult daughter Lolly arrives and resents Nellie's devotion to the rabbit. Seeing only a toy, she takes Edward away and throws him into the rubbish. Edward loses a second loving home just as he has begun to understand its value. Buried among refuse, he can do nothing but wait and remember the people from whom he has been separated.

A dog named Lucy digs Edward out of the rubbish and carries him to her companion, a wanderer called Bull. Bull names the rabbit Malone and welcomes him beside the campfires of people who travel without homes. Edward rides the rails with Bull and Lucy for years, hearing the travelers name and remember those they miss. For the first time he understands that loss is shared by many people and that remembering someone can itself be an act of love. A railway guard eventually discovers the group and kicks Edward from the moving train. Once again he is separated without warning from those he has come to love. His wider experience has made him capable of grief, leaving each new abandonment more painful than the last.

After further neglect, Edward is hung on a pole as a scarecrow. A poor boy named Bryce releases him and carries him home to Sarah Ruth, Bryce's little sister, who is gravely ill. Sarah Ruth names the rabbit Jangles and holds him close. Bryce works while trying to care for her, and Edward recognizes the depth of the siblings' love and the danger of losing it. Sarah Ruth's health worsens despite Bryce's efforts. Edward can neither speak nor act, but he now loves the child and suffers with her rather than observing her pain from a distance. When Sarah Ruth dies, Bryce and Edward are left together in grief, and Bryce takes the rabbit with him as he tries to find a way forward.

Bryce reaches Memphis and tries to earn money by making Edward dance on strings for passersby. At a diner he orders food he cannot pay for. The owner reacts by swinging Edward down onto a counter, shattering the rabbit's china head. In the darkness that follows, Edward hears voices associated with those he has lost and must choose whether to continue. He wakes repaired in the workshop of Lucius Clarke, a doll mender. Bryce cannot pay the repair bill, and Lucius keeps Edward, separating the boy from the last companion tied to Sarah Ruth. Restored physically but exhausted by repeated loss, Edward sits among the dolls in the shop and decides that loving anyone has brought only pain.

Edward remains for years on a shelf in Lucius Clarke's shop, watching other dolls be chosen while he refuses to hope. An old doll waiting beside him argues that keeping one's heart closed guarantees that no one can arrive. After she is bought, Edward is alone with that lesson. A young girl named Maggie eventually enters and wants him. Her mother examines the rabbit and recognizes him as the Edward she lost at sea: she is Abilene, now grown. Edward recognizes her as well, and the familiar pocket watch and his distinctive construction confirm the reunion. Maggie takes Edward into the next generation of the Tulane family. Returned to his first owner after his many transformations, Edward is no longer the indifferent rabbit Pellegrina warned. He has learned that love exposes him to grief, yet is willing to open himself to it.

characters.description: An uncompromising nobleman who despises social flattery and insists on complete sincerity. His principles repeatedly bring him into conflict with polite society, yet he is passionately attached to the fashionable Célimène.
characters.name: Alceste

characters.description: Alceste's even-tempered friend. He believes courtesy and small accommodations are necessary for people to live together and tries to moderate Alceste's rigid judgments.
characters.name: Philinte

characters.description: A fashionable young widow with many admirers, including Alceste. Quick-witted and socially skilled, she enjoys company, gossip, and the freedom of postponing a choice among her suitors.
characters.name: Célimène

characters.description: A courtier and aspiring poet who asks Alceste for a candid opinion of his sonnet. He expects admiration, and Alceste's refusal to provide it turns literary vanity into a formal dispute.
characters.name: Oronte

characters.description: Célimène's sensible cousin and another possible match for Alceste. She understands his better qualities without sharing his hostility toward ordinary social conduct.
characters.name: Éliante

characters.description: A self-righteous woman who presents herself as morally severe and claims concern for Célimène's reputation. Her interest in Alceste gives her visit a personal purpose as well as a social one.
characters.name: Arsinoé

characters.description: One of the fashionable marquesses who gathers at Célimène's house and competes for her attention. He joins readily in the clever judgments made about absent acquaintances.
characters.name: Acaste

characters.description: A courtly marquess and one of Célimène's persistent admirers. He treats the rivalry for her favor as part of fashionable social life.
characters.name: Clitandre

characters.description: Alceste's servant, whose hurried warning about his master's legal troubles interrupts the disputes at Célimène's house.
characters.name: Du Bois

recaps.ending: Letters written by Célimène expose that she has privately encouraged several suitors while ridiculing each of them to the others. Oronte, Acaste, and Clitandre withdraw after hearing the evidence. Alceste is willing to forgive Célimène if she will marry him and leave society for a secluded life, but she refuses the isolation he demands. He therefore renounces their relationship. Arsinoé offers herself as an alternative and is sharply dismissed. Éliante accepts Philinte's proposal, and the two decide to follow Alceste and try to keep him from carrying out his plan to abandon society. Alceste ends morally consistent but alone, unable to reconcile his demand for absolute truth with either love or ordinary social life.
recaps.in_short: Alceste condemns the polite insincerity practiced by his friend Philinte and the fashionable circle around Célimène, the witty young widow he loves. His refusal to praise Oronte's sonnet creates an official quarrel, while his jealousy grows as Célimène entertains several suitors. Arsinoé, who desires Alceste, promises evidence that Célimène is unfaithful. A compromising letter appears, but Célimène initially explains it away. Alceste then loses an unrelated lawsuit and resolves to leave society. When letters circulated among Célimène's admirers reveal that she has encouraged each man while mocking all the others, most suitors abandon her. Alceste offers forgiveness only if she will marry him and share his complete retreat from the world. She refuses that condition, so he leaves alone. Philinte and Éliante agree to marry and go after him, hoping to prevent his self-imposed exile.

recaps.text: Alceste rebukes his friend Philinte for warmly greeting a man he scarcely knows. Philinte argues that ordinary courtesy keeps society workable, while Alceste demands that outward conduct exactly match inward feeling. Their debate also exposes a contradiction: Alceste loves Célimène, a young widow celebrated for the social graces he condemns, while the more compatible Éliante cares for him. Oronte arrives seeking friendship and an honest judgment of his new sonnet. Alceste tries to discourage him indirectly, then finally declares the poem poor. Offended, Oronte quarrels with him, and their disagreement is referred to the authorities for settlement.

Alceste presses Célimène to choose him and stop encouraging other admirers. She dismisses his jealousy and insists that social attentions do not prove love. Their argument is interrupted as Éliante, the marquesses Acaste and Clitandre, and other visitors gather. Célimène entertains them with sharp portraits of absent acquaintances, delighting everyone except Alceste, who sees their approval as another form of hypocrisy. He refuses to flatter her even when challenged and accuses the group of rewarding her faults. A guard then summons him to answer the complaint arising from his criticism of Oronte's sonnet, forcing him to leave the romantic dispute unresolved.

Arsinoé visits Célimène under the guise of friendship and reports that respectable society criticizes her conduct with men. Célimène answers by describing the equally unkind judgments made about Arsinoé's severity and self-advertised virtue. Once Célimène leaves, Arsinoé turns to Alceste. She praises his merit, suggests that she can help him at court, and criticizes his devotion to a woman who does not deserve his trust. Alceste rejects court advancement and asks for facts rather than insinuation. Arsinoé promises to show him direct evidence of Célimène's disloyalty and leads him away to see it.

Philinte and Éliante discuss Alceste's difficult love, and Philinte admits that he would gladly marry Éliante if Alceste remains fixed on Célimène. Alceste arrives with a letter supplied by Arsinoé that appears to show Célimène favoring Oronte. He confronts Célimène and turns even his pain into an argument for her to confess plainly. She challenges his interpretation and manages to restore enough uncertainty that he remains attached to her. Before the matter is settled, Alceste's servant Du Bois brings alarming news about a separate lawsuit. Alceste has lost the case despite believing the justice wholly on his side, and further trouble may follow. He resolves to withdraw from a society that, to him, has proved corrupt in both love and law.

After losing his lawsuit, Alceste declares that he will leave society and asks Célimène to share his retreat. Oronte also demands that she choose between them. Acaste and Clitandre then produce letters in which Célimène has privately encouraged her various admirers while mocking each of the others. Confronted with the matching evidence, she no longer attempts a full denial. Oronte and the marquesses abandon their courtship. Alceste says he will forgive her if she marries him and lives apart from the world, but Célimène will not accept such isolation. He ends their relationship. Arsinoé tries to offer herself and is rejected as well. Éliante accepts Philinte's love, and they plan to pursue Alceste in the hope of stopping his complete withdrawal. Alceste departs consistent in his principles but separated from the people who still care for him.
